summary: Describes Simple Virtual Aggregation (S-VA), a technique that lets some BGP routers avoid installing every route from the default-free routing table into their forwarding table. The idea is to reduce forwarding table size. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of every mailbox carrying a map of every street, some boxes get a shorter map and send hard questions to ones that know more.

subtitle: Reduce routing table size using virtual aggregation prefixes.

tldr.problem: Edge routers in large networks must carry the full routing table to reach all destinations, but storing millions of routes consumes significant memory and processing resources.
tldr.mechanism: Core routers announce a virtual aggregate prefix with a specific next-hop, and edge routers suppress storage of more-specific routes that point to the same next-hop, installing only the aggregate.
tldr.outcome: Edge routers can operate with significantly smaller forwarding information bases while maintaining full connectivity, reducing operational costs.

today: RFC 6769 is an Informational memo that remains valid guidance for operators seeking to optimize edge router memory usage through virtual aggregation. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: The Routing Table Size Problem
sections.content:
The global routing table has grown to millions of prefixes (IP address ranges). Routers in the Default-Free Zone must carry nearly all of them to deliver traffic to any destination. This exhausts memory on edge routers and increases lookup latency. Simple Virtual Aggregation (S-VA) is a technique that allows some routers to operate without storing all routes, while still advertising and receiving the full routing table via BGP.

S-VA is purely local to a single autonomous system. It requires no inter-domain negotiation, no tunneling, and no changes to routers that do not support it. It relies only on existing BGP functionality.
sections.plainLanguage: Modern routers are drowning in information about every network in the world. S-VA lets some routers get away with less detail.

sections.title: How S-VA Works
sections.content:
S-VA defines two types of routers. FIB-Installing Routers (FIR) maintain the complete forwarding table and advertise virtual aggregate (VA) prefixes alongside normal routes. FIB-Suppressing Routers (FSR) receive all routes via BGP but suppress installation into the forwarding table of any more-specific routes that have the same next-hop as the VA prefix.

The VA prefix is typically the default route (0/0) or a large block, and the FIR sets its next-hop attribute to point toward itself. When an FSR receives both the VA prefix and a more-specific route pointing to the same next-hop, it installs only the VA prefix. Traffic destined for the more-specific routes follows the VA prefix to the FIR, which then forwards using the more-specific route.
sections.plainLanguage: One smart router says 'I know the whole map', and edge routers say 'I'll just remember that one route and ask you about details when I need them'.

sections.title: Deployment Model
sections.content:
Typically, AS boundary routers (ASBRs) are configured as FIRs, and customer-facing edge routers are configured as FSRs. The FIR announces one or more VA prefixes with NO_EXPORT community to ensure they remain within the AS. An FSR may have a default route to the FIR or to a point-of-presence (POP) boundary router.

Multiple FIRs can announce different VA prefixes, or the same VA prefix. An FSR will suppress routes based on whichever VA prefix it installs. When internal BGP multipath is enabled, the FSR uses the set of next-hops from the VA prefix multipath to determine which more-specific routes to suppress. This enables traffic splitting among redundant exit routers.
sections.plainLanguage: The backbone routers advertise 'I have all the routes', and edge routers listen and discard their local copies of redundant information.

sections.title: Operational Considerations
sections.content:
Operators must be aware of several edge cases. If a BGP route is used to resolve the next-hop of another route or is redistributed to other protocols, suppression into the forwarding table may break redistribution. The solution is to suppress from the FIB only, not from the RIB. When an FSR originates a route or aggregate that does not fully correspond to received routes, unreachable addresses within the aggregate may result in packets being sent to the FIR.

If a VA prefix changes next-hop or is withdrawn, many suppressed routes must be installed quickly to maintain convergence. The FIR SHOULD NOT suppress any routes, and should use ORIGIN INCOMPLETE to signal aggregation. No ATOMIC_AGGREGATE or AGGREGATOR attributes should be included on the VA prefix announcement.
sections.plainLanguage: The system works smoothly when everyone follows the rules about how to announce these aggregate routes and what happens when they change.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
S-VA has no known security vulnerabilities beyond those of normal BGP. The local nature of the optimization means it creates no external exposure. More-specific routes may be present as normal BGP behavior, and the suppression is transparent to external routers. An operator might use GTSM (Generalized TTL Security Mechanism) to protect IBGP sessions, as with any internal BGP deployment.

Because S-VA operates entirely within an AS and is invisible to other networks, it does not introduce new attack surfaces or require additional security infrastructure.
sections.plainLanguage: This optimization does not introduce any new ways for attackers to compromise routers beyond normal BGP attacks.
